From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Overall assessment

**The Seller’s package should not be accepted as drafted.** It combines broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with limitations applying to almost every claim. That could leave Wattlebridge paying the full AUD 24 million while bearing known pre-Completion liabilities and having little effective recourse.

The principal priorities are:

1. **Do not complete without effective Bluefen consent and Riverlark repayment/security releases.**
2. **Ensure the funds flow delivers the agreed debt-free/cash-free economics**, including proper treatment of Completion bonuses.
3. **Resolve Ironquay ownership and protect against the identified incident**, rather than relying on warranties that the disclosures may qualify.
4. **Separate fundamental, tax and specific indemnity protection from the general warranty limitations.**
5. **Reject blanket data-room disclosure and constructive Buyer knowledge.**

This assessment is based on the Seller’s summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. Those documents need checking before settling amendments.

## 1. Liability limitations could defeat the protections being negotiated

**Seller position:** General warranty liability is capped at AUD 4.8 million, with a AUD 25,000 de minimis, AUD 250,000 deductible basket and 18-month notification period. Limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly excluded.

**Why this matters:** The commercial effect is cumulative. Even an otherwise valid claim may be excluded by disclosure or knowledge, reduced by the basket, and then capped. Applying this framework to all Claims could also restrict recovery for failure to deliver title, breach of Completion obligations, unpaid debt, tax and specific indemnities.

**Push back:**

- Apply the general warranty regime **only to expressly defined general warranty claims**. Do not rely on scattered exceptions.
- Establish separate regimes for fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and other contractual obligations.
- Seek a higher general warranty cap and longer notification period—**24–36 months is a reasonable Buyer opening position**, subject to the overall risk allocation and any insurance.
- Reduce the de minimis and basket; seek a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying losses are recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.
- Aggregate claims arising from the same or related facts so they cannot be fragmented below the threshold.
- Permit notification of contingent claims and reasonable estimates. Check for short proceedings deadlines, overly technical notice requirements and other claim-extinguishing provisions in the complete SPA.

The proposed figures are negotiation positions, not inherently invalid terms. Their adequacy depends on the protections retained elsewhere.

## 2. Fundamental warranties, tax and fraud need distinct treatment

**Seller position:** Capacity and title receive the same cap and time limit as general warranties; tax and IP are said to be “settled” under that regime.

**Why this matters:** A 20% recovery ceiling is inadequate if Wattlebridge does not acquire the shares or the Seller lacked authority to sell them. Tax liabilities can emerge well after 18 months. The Seller’s assertion that these matters are settled does not establish Buyer agreement.

**Push back:**

- Give title, capacity, authority and freedom-from-encumbrances warranties a separate cap of **at least the purchase price**, without de minimis or basket, and a materially longer claim period.
- Obtain a dedicated tax covenant/indemnity allocating pre-Completion tax to the Seller, with appropriate assessment-period coverage, extensions and tax-specific claims procedures.
- Consider enhanced protection for business-critical IP warranties, separately from the known Ironquay issue.
- Expressly preserve claims for Seller fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation and deliberate concealment, including appropriate attribution for relevant representatives.
- Preserve rights and liabilities that cannot lawfully be excluded.

NSW law does not make broad limitation or non-reliance clauses automatically ineffective. The Buyer should negotiate express protection rather than expect a court to rescue an unfavourable bargain.

## 3. Blanket disclosure and deemed knowledge would transfer diligence risk to the Buyer

**Seller position:** Everything contained or referred to in the data room, accounts, statutory registers and public records is disclosed. Buyer knowledge includes advisers’ knowledge and matters merely discoverable from those sources.

**Why this matters:** “Referred to” and “discoverable” extend beyond information actually supplied and understood. Together, these provisions could convert incomplete diligence into a defence to almost any warranty claim.

**Push back:**

- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter**.
- Reject wholesale disclosure of the data room and public registers. Any agreed general disclosures should be narrow and precisely identified.
- Require specific disclosures against identified warranties and a frozen, indexed copy of the disclosed materials.
- Delete constructive/imputed knowledge and automatic attribution of advisers’ knowledge. If a knowledge exclusion is agreed, limit it to actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, with no duty to investigate.
- Ensure disclosure and knowledge **do not qualify specific indemnities, price adjustments, debt repayment obligations or Completion conditions**, unless expressly agreed.
- Require updates through Completion, but do not let unilateral updates automatically cure breaches or remove Buyer termination rights.

For known issues, warranties alone are not enough: secure an express cure obligation, price treatment or indemnity.

## 4. Bluefen: consent must be effective and its conditions satisfied

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours, with the condition satisfied on delivery of written consent.

**Risk:** Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue. The Disclosure Letter confirms there is no final consent or evidence that associated conditions are satisfied. A conditional consent may leave the Company exposed to termination, repricing or other adverse terms.

**Push back:**

- Make **valid, effective consent and satisfaction of its associated conditions** a condition precedent for the Buyer’s benefit.
- Require the consent to cover the actual transaction and avoid materially adverse amendments, fees, waivers or concessions without Buyer approval.
- Require supporting evidence, cooperation and prompt progress reporting.
- Include a long-stop date and Buyer termination right if the condition is not met; only the Buyer should be able to waive it.

Reasonable endeavours may govern the Seller’s efforts. They should not replace the required outcome.

## 5. Riverlark: post-Completion release is not adequate

**Seller position:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding; release follows Completion.

**Risk:** The Buyer could acquire a company still owing acquisition-sensitive debt and subject to enforceable security. That is inconsistent with a debt-free acquisition unless fully addressed in the agreed mechanics.

**Push back:**

- Obtain a current payout letter covering principal, accrued interest, fees and break costs, plus the necessary change-control waiver or consent.
- Repay the lender directly through the Completion funds flow.
- Require binding discharge arrangements effective at Completion, covering all relevant securities, guarantees and registrations.
- Permit later administrative registration steps only where repayment and the lender’s release obligations are already secured.
- Confirm the debt deduction or discharge allocation in the price mechanics **without double counting**.

The AUD 3.2 million is approximate, not a final payout figure.

## 6. Completion bonuses: a real funds-flow gap

**Seller position:** AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” but omitted from the funds flow.

**Risk:** If the Company is liable, Wattlebridge may inherit the payment obligation even though the Seller describes it as its own cost. Additional employment on-costs may apply.

**Push back:**

- Confirm the obligor, recipients, entitlement conditions, payment timing and whether continued employment is measured beyond Completion.
- Allocate transaction-triggered bonuses to the Seller through direct funding, a debt-like deduction or another express mechanism.
- Determine and include applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other employer on-costs; properly address withholding.
- Provide for conditional amounts through a retention or true-up where appropriate.
- Prevent double counting against working capital or another adjustment.

Do not treat AUD 420,000 as a fully quantified, unconditional liability—but do not leave it unallocated.

## 7. Ironquay: paying an invoice and obtaining IP ownership are different protections

**Seller position:** The indemnity covers only the specific SOW3 payment. Records show AUD 180,000 open, but do not independently prove non-payment.

**Risk:** Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The issue is potentially defective IP ownership, not merely an unpaid invoice.

**Push back:**

- Verify all SOW3 amounts and payment status; obtain cleared-payment evidence.
- Require a confirmatory assignment and appropriate releases from the relevant rights holder, covering the materials and rights the Company needs.
- Check the underlying chain of title, third-party components and any residual restrictions.
- Expand the specific indemnity beyond the invoice to losses arising from pre-Completion non-payment or defective title, including reasonable defence, settlement and remediation costs.
- Keep that indemnity outside general warranty disclosure, knowledge, basket and cap provisions, under a separately negotiated regime.

If the materials are business-critical, cure should be a Completion requirement, not merely a post-Completion damages remedy.

## 8. Export/privacy incident: investigate before accepting the Seller’s assessment

**Seller position:** Preliminary and not expected to be material.

**Risk:** The records establish a misdirected download link and a possible export of approximately 1,240 records. They do **not** establish unauthorised access, the exact scope, a notifiable breach or a loss amount. Neither reassurance nor a definitive breach conclusion is justified yet.

**Push back:**

- Obtain access logs, link permissions and expiry details, the actual dataset, containment steps and investigation findings.
- Assess applicable privacy, contractual notification and security obligations, including whether Australian eligible-data-breach requirements apply.
- Require prompt containment, evidence preservation, lawful notifications where required and Buyer involvement in material decisions.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the identified pre-Completion incident, with appropriate claims procedures and duration.
- Consider a targeted retention if residual exposure remains unresolved and material.

Reject the unsupported immateriality assessment, without overstating the evidence.

## 9. Sandbar renewals: investigate classification before allocating AUD 330,000

Three related AUD 110,000 renewals should be assessed together. Calling them ordinary-course costs does not establish that treatment.

Check execution and renewal dates, cancellation rights, service periods, accruals, budget treatment and commercial necessity. Depending on those facts, the amounts may be ordinary operating expenditure, working-capital liabilities, debt-like items or commitments requiring Buyer approval.

**Push back:** prohibit new or accelerated commitments outside agreed ordinary-course limits; allocate existing liabilities consistently with the price definitions. Do not automatically deduct the full AUD 330,000 simply because it is disclosed.

## 10. Title, lease and Mossvale require accurate—not inflated—treatment

- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, but the register alone does not resolve every ownership or encumbrance risk. Verify the issued capital, transfers and allotments, options or other rights, security interests, transfer restrictions and required corporate approvals. Require effective Completion transfers and full fundamental warranties.
- **Office lease:** The disclosed obligation is notification, not landlord consent. Require timely compliant notice and check consequences of non-compliance; do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not, by itself, require consent to a share sale. Review the complete provision for change-control, deemed-assignment or termination wording before requiring consent.

## Recommended negotiating position

| Priority | Buyer requirement |
|---|---|
| **Completion gates** | Effective Bluefen consent with conditions satisfied; Riverlark payout and effective releases; Ironquay cure if business-critical. |
| **Price protection** | Reconciled debt-free/cash-free funds flow; express allocation of bonuses and applicable on-costs; evidence-based treatment of renewals. |
| **Known-risk protection** | Specific Ironquay and incident protections that survive disclosure and Buyer knowledge. |
| **Recourse** | Separate fundamental, tax and indemnity regimes; appropriate fraud carve-outs; improved general warranty limitations. |
| **Disclosure discipline** | Fair, specific disclosure; no blanket discoverability standard or adviser-knowledge exclusion. |

**Bottom line:** settle the actual Completion deliverables and economic allocations first. A higher warranty cap is of limited value if the known risks are disclosed away, attributed to Buyer knowledge, or caught by an all-claims exclusion.
